The diagnosis

Monday, 20 June 2033. The heatwave has lasted ten days. The city botanist, Dr Claire Lefèvre, has come to examine the lime tree next to the Salle Hélène Morel, which is losing its leaves. Julien is with her.
Right, I’ve finished my measurements. Your lime tree is suffering, that’s certain.
Is it because of the heat?
Partly. As it hasn’t rained for six weeks, the ground is dry to a depth of one metre.
But the other trees in the park seem to be fine.
Because they’re old. Their roots go very deep to find water. Yours was planted three years ago: for lack of deep roots, it has no reserves.
Since it’s thirsty, all we have to do is water it, isn’t it?
In theory, yes. But public watering is banned owing to the drought.
Even to save a tree?
Even for that. Given that the city’s water reserves are at their lowest, the prefecture makes no exceptions.
That’s absurd. It’s going to die of thirst on the pretext that it’s in a public garden?
I understand. But it’s not that the law is stupid: it’s that there isn’t enough water for everyone.
Then how do we save it?
With water that doesn’t come from the mains. If you find some, it has a chance. By watering it every evening, we can keep it alive until the rain.
I’ll talk to someone. She always finds solutions.

1. The basic conjunctions: parce que, car, comme, puisque
All four introduce a cause, but they have different positions and nuances:
Position / nuance
after the verb; answers “pourquoi ?”
Ils vont bien parce qu’ils sont vieux.
after a comma; written register
L’arbre souffre, car il ne pleut plus.
AT THE START of the sentence
Comme il ne pleut plus, la terre est sèche.
known, obvious cause
Puisqu’il a soif, il faut l’arroser.
Causal “comme” always comes at the start of the sentence. “La terre est sèche comme il ne pleut plus” ✗. And “car” can never come at the start.
2. Prepositions: grâce à, à cause de, en raison de
They are all followed by a NOUN. The difference lies in the nuance of the cause:
Preposition
positive cause (good result)
Grâce à la pluie, l’arbre a survécu.
negative cause (bad result)
Il souffre à cause de la sécheresse.
neutral, formal (official notices)
L’arrosage est interdit en raison de la sécheresse.
du fait de
neutral, formal
Du fait de la chaleur, les écoles ferment.
Careful: “grâce à” with a negative result sounds ironic! “Grâce à toi, on a raté le train.” = “Thanks to you, we missed the train.”
3. Faute de, à force de, étant donné que
For lack of deep roots, it has no reserves. (faute de + noun without article)
If you don’t water it, the tree will die. (faute de + infinitive)
By watering it again and again, we saved it. (repetition, effort)
Given that reserves are low, no exception is made.
“Vu que” and “du fait que” mean the same as “étant donné que”. “Vu que” is more informal, “du fait que” more formal.
4. False or rejected cause
When you dispute a cause or present it as an excuse, you use:
It’s going to die on the pretext that it’s in a public garden? (+ indicative)
It’s not that the law is stupid, it’s that there isn’t enough water. (+ subjunctive, then indicative)
Not that it’s cold, but it’s raining. (elevated register)
After “ce n’est pas que” and “non que” comes the SUBJUNCTIVE, because you are rejecting the cause. The second part (“c’est que…”) goes back to the indicative.
5. Cause without a conjunction: pour + past infinitive, de + noun
pour + past infinitive
Il a été puni pour avoir menti.
He was punished for lying.
pour + noun
Elle a été félicitée pour son courage.
She was congratulated on her courage.
de + noun
Il va mourir de soif.
He’s going to die of thirst.
Elle tremblait de froid.
She was shaking with cold.
Étant trop jeune, il n’a pas de réserves.

L’été où les tilleuls ont eu soif

The summer of 2033 began early. From 10 June, the thermometer topped thirty-five degrees in Lyon, and it didn’t come down again for nine weeks. The newspapers talked about the worst heatwave since records began. Schools closed in the afternoons. Old people stayed indoors with the shutters closed. And on the hills around the city, the grass had turned yellow, then grey, then almost white, like straw.

On rue d’Austerlitz, the flat had become an oven. Henri-Ion, who was two and a half, no longer slept. He cried all night, red and sweaty, pushing away his sheets. Ioana and Julien had tried fans, wet towels, cold showers at midnight. Nothing worked. In the end it was Isabelle who found the solution: thanks to the thick walls of the old building, her flat, overlooking the courtyard, stayed four degrees cooler.

So all summer the children slept on the other side of the landing, in Odile’s old room, on mattresses on the floor. The door between the two flats stayed open day and night. In the evenings, Isabelle read them stories about snow and mountains, to cool them down, she said. Henri-Ion fell asleep in the middle of the second page. Rose-Hélène always demanded the ending.

In Iași it was even hotter. Grandma called every evening to give advice. Close the shutters at six in the morning. Hang wet sheets in front of the windows. Eat cold food. Don’t go out between noon and five. She said she had lived through the summer of 1946, when the village wells had dried up, and nobody had air conditioning back then. People survived all the same, through patience and cool water.

Rose-Hélène, who was five and three months, was the first to notice that something was wrong. One Saturday morning, coming back from the market, she had stopped in front of the La Duchère lime tree, the one under which a handful of Odile’s ashes rested. She had looked up. Then she had tugged at her father’s sleeve. “Daddy,” she had said, “the tree’s leaves are falling. But it isn’t autumn.”

Julien looked. She was right. The lime tree’s leaves, normally a deep green in June, were yellowed at the edges, curled up, and many had already fallen on the scorched ground. The tree looked tired, almost ill. Julien touched the bark. It was dry and hot, like a stone in the sun. He felt a worry he didn’t show his daughter.

Throughout the network, the heat was upsetting rehearsals. In Marseille, Nice and Toulouse, it was over forty degrees in the halls in the afternoon. The children almost fainted on their chairs. Julien made a decision that surprised everyone: all summer rehearsals would take place at seven in the morning. The parents protested for a week. Then they noticed their children came home in a good mood, and they fell silent.

On Monday he called the city’s parks department. He was put through to a botanist, Dr Claire Lefèvre, who looked after the trees of the whole north-west of Lyon. She came the same day. She was a woman of about forty, in shorts and a straw hat, with a rucksack full of strange instruments. She walked around the lime tree three times without a word, taking notes.

Later, Julien would learn that Dr Lefèvre had grown up in the Vaucluse, on a farm where her father grew cherry trees. During the drought of 2022, for lack of water, half the orchard had died in a single summer. She was fifteen. She had seen her father cry in front of the dried-up trees. It was because of that summer, she said, that she had become a botanist. To understand. And so that it wouldn’t happen again.

Then she pushed a long metal probe into the ground at the foot of the tree. She looked at the screen. She pulled a face. “The ground is dry to a depth of one metre,” she said. “This lime tree is suffering because of the drought, obviously. But not only that. As it was planted less than three years ago, its roots aren’t yet deep enough to reach the water. It’s young. It has no reserves.”

Julien asked whether it would die. The botanist hesitated. She said it depended on the summer. If the heatwave lasted another month without rain, it was possible. It would need watering, a lot, regularly, in the evening, when the heat dropped. But there was a problem: owing to the drought, the prefecture had just banned the watering of public green spaces. The city’s water reserves were at their lowest.

That evening, Julien told them all this at dinner. Rose-Hélène listened very carefully. She didn’t understand everything, especially the word “prefecture”. But she understood the essential thing: Odile’s tree was thirsty, and nobody was allowed to give it a drink. She put down her fork. She said it was the stupidest law she had ever heard. Ioana didn’t dare contradict her.

The next day, Julien called Amina. Amina called the prefecture. The prefecture replied that no exception was possible, for lack of sufficient reserves. Amina then asked a very precise question: did the ban concern water from the public mains, or any water? The official checked. It concerned water from the public mains. Collected rainwater, for example, was not affected. Amina hung up. She opened a spreadsheet.

The problem, of course, was that it hadn’t rained for six weeks. There was no rainwater to collect. But Amina had another idea. She had noticed that in all the La Duchère tower blocks, the air conditioners ran day and night because of the heat. And that each air conditioner discharged condensation water through a small pipe. Litres and litres of clean water, going down the drains every day.

She asked the botanist whether that water was suitable for a tree. Dr Lefèvre thought, then said yes: it was distilled water, almost pure, with no limescale or chlorine. It wasn’t ideal in the long term, but to save a tree in the middle of a heatwave, it was perfect. She added, smiling, that nobody had ever asked her that question in twenty years of her career.

Now the water had to be collected. Amina had a poster printed, which the orchestra children stuck up in every building entrance in the neighbourhood: “Is your air conditioner crying? Don’t waste its tears! Bring the condensation water to the lime tree by the Salle Hélène Morel, every evening at eight. The lime tree thanks you.” Inès had written the text. Rose-Hélène had drawn a tree drinking through a straw.

The first evening, Thursday 23 June, three people came. The baker, with two buckets. Nadia, Inès’s mother, with a five-litre bottle. And the school caretaker, with a watering can. Rose-Hélène was waiting for them under the tree with her own little red watering can, the one from the planting in the Parc de la Tête d’Or. They poured the water at the foot of the lime tree, slowly, so that it would soak in. It was barely twenty litres. It was nothing.

The second evening there were eleven of them. The third, twenty-eight. Word of mouth had done its work. After a week, every evening at eight, a queue formed outside the Salle Hélène Morel: children, parents, grandmothers, teenagers, each with a bucket, a bottle or a saucepan full of air-conditioner water. Some came from the other end of the neighbourhood. An old man pushed a supermarket trolley loaded with jerrycans.

Amina kept count, of course. She was there every evening, standing next to the tree, phone in hand, and recorded every litre in a spreadsheet. Dr Lefèvre had told her the lime tree needed about a hundred litres an evening to survive. On 30 June they reached a hundred and twelve litres. On 5 July, two hundred and thirty. Amina had to ask people to pour the water more slowly, so it wouldn’t overflow.

The evening water distribution had become a neighbourhood meeting point. People who had lived in the same building for twenty years without ever speaking found themselves side by side, bucket in hand, waiting their turn. An old Algerian gentleman on the eighth floor discovered that the young mother on the ground floor came from the same village as his grandmother. They talked for an hour. The next day he brought her dates.

On Thursdays, after the adult orchestra’s rehearsal, Mr Vidal stayed to help Amina count the litres. He missed his 21:34 train and took the 22:34. He said it was to check her figures, out of professional habit. Amina made no comment. But she had added a column to her spreadsheet, headed “Check B. V.”, where she noted his figures next to hers. They were always identical.

Rose-Hélène, for her part, had turned the holiday club into a water-collection centre. She had persuaded the leaders to leave basins under the building’s air conditioners, and every evening the children brought the water back in plastic bottles. She kept a tally too, on a sheet of paper, with sticks to count the bottles. Amina had looked at it with great respect. She had said it was an excellent start.

The lime tree took its time to respond. For two weeks it went on losing its leaves. Rose-Hélène came to check every morning before going to the holiday club. She counted the leaves that had fallen during the night. Then, on 8 July, she came running home, out of breath, red in the face, shouting so loudly that Henri-Ion started to cry. At the end of a low branch she had found a small new leaf. Tender green.

Dr Lefèvre came to confirm it the next day. The lime tree was putting out new leaves. It wasn’t won yet, but it was a good sign: thanks to the air-conditioner water, its roots had regained enough moisture to restart growth. She measured the soil moisture. She smiled. Then she told Amina that in her next report to the town hall, she would cite the La Duchère method as an example. Amina asked whether she could have a copy of the report.

Inès had written an article for her lycée newspaper about air-conditioner water. The school paper published it. Then the neighbourhood paper picked it up. Then a big regional daily. In three days, dozens of neighbourhoods in France copied the La Duchère method. In Grenoble, Mrs Faure had buckets put under all the town hall’s air conditioners to water the plane trees on rue des Tanneurs.

But while La Duchère was saving its tree, other news arrived, much more worrying. On 12 July, on the evening news, Julien saw pictures of a fire in Corsica. A huge forest fire, caused by the heat and fanned by a violent wind, was ravaging the mountains above Corte. Whole villages were being evacuated. On the screen, Julien recognised the little square of a village he knew well.

It was Antoine’s village. The old Corsican shepherd, now ninety-six, who had planted the network’s twelfth lime tree in June 2031 to the singing of the three village women. Julien immediately called the music teacher in Corte. Nobody answered. He called the village town hall. Nobody. He spent the evening calling every number he had, with no result.

It was only around midnight that his phone rang. It was the music teacher, exhausted, his voice hoarse. He was calling from a sports hall in Corte where the evacuated residents had been housed. Everyone was safe and sound. Antoine too, despite his age. But he had refused to leave for hours. The firefighters had had to carry him to the truck. He didn’t want to abandon his tree.

The next day they learnt that the fire had reached the village during the night. Several houses had burnt down. The school too. And the little square, with its stone wash house, its fountain and its young lime tree, was in the middle of the devastated area. Nobody knew yet what was left of it. The firefighters were blocking access to the village, because the fire was still smouldering under the ashes and trees might fall.

The Corte fire captain explained on television how the fire had started. A cigarette thrown from a car at the roadside, into the dry grass. Because of the wind, blowing at more than eighty kilometres an hour, the flames had leapt from one hill to the next in a few minutes. And for lack of rain for two months, the forest had burnt like paper. “It’s not that we were short of men,” he said. “It’s that nature was ready to burn.”

They had to wait five days. On 18 July, the music teacher was finally able to enter the village with the firefighters. He sent Julien a series of photos without comment. Blackened walls. Collapsed roofs. Burnt-out cars. The school, of which only the walls remained. And then, in the last photo, the little square. The wash house was intact. So was the fountain. And in the middle, the lime tree.

It was black. Its leaves had burnt completely. Its trunk was charred on one side, up to a man’s height. It looked dead. Julien looked at the photo for a long time without a word. Then he showed it to Ioana. Ioana put her hand to her mouth. Rose-Hélène, looking over her mother’s shoulder, asked what it was. Julien hesitated. Then he told the truth. Rose-Hélène didn’t cry. She asked whether they could water it.

Julien called Dr Lefèvre. He sent her the photo. She called back an hour later. She had consulted a colleague who specialised in Mediterranean fires. Their conclusion was cautious. A burnt lime tree was not necessarily dead. Since the bark was charred on one side only, the vessels carrying the sap might still work on the other side. If the roots had survived, the tree might come back. But they would have to wait until spring to know.

The problem, she added, was water. After a fire, the burnt earth no longer held moisture, and on the pretext that the tree looked dead, nobody would bother to water it. Yet it was precisely now that it needed it most. Someone on site would have to water it every week until the first autumn rains. Julien hung up. He already knew who would do it.

Antoine, of course. As soon as the residents were allowed back, on 24 July, the old shepherd returned to the village in his grandson’s van. His house had half burnt down. He didn’t complain. He asked for a bucket. He went to the fountain, which was still running, fed by a mountain spring the fire hadn’t touched. He filled the bucket. And he watered the lime tree.

He did it every day. At ninety-six, his cane in one hand and his bucket in the other, he made six trips between the fountain and the tree every morning, before the heat became unbearable. The villagers watched him with a mixture of respect and pity. Some thought he had lost his mind because of the shock. A neighbour kindly told him the tree was dead. Antoine replied: “You don’t know that. Neither do I. So I water it.”

After a week, the three village women, the ones who had sung on the day of the planting, came to help him. They too had lost part of their houses. They carried the buckets while Antoine poured the water. And while he poured, they sang. The same polyphonic song as in June 2031. Slowly, in three voices, on the blackened square, among the ruins, every morning.

A Corse-Matin journalist who had come to report on the burnt villages came across the scene by chance. He filmed from a distance, without disturbing them: the old man, the three women, the bucket, the song, the black tree. He published the video that same evening with a very simple title: “They water a dead tree”. The next day it had been viewed five hundred thousand times. The following week, three million.

In Lyon, at the Fabre & Popescu firm, Ioana saw the video the next morning. She showed it to Sorina and Hugo. They looked at the burnt school behind the old man with his bucket. They didn’t need to discuss it. That same evening, Ioana wrote to the village town hall: her firm offered to draw up the plans for the new school, with its music room, free of charge. The mayor replied in one line: “Come whenever you like.”

Amina, of course, took care of the donations. In a week, more than four thousand people had sent money to rebuild the village school. She opened a spreadsheet with a column for every donation, even the smallest. There was a two-euro donation sent by a child from Lille, with a message: “For the buckets.” Amina printed it out. She pinned it above her desk, next to Mr Vidal’s card.

Responses came from everywhere. People offered to send money to rebuild the school. Nurseries offered a new lime tree. Antoine refused the new lime tree. He said you don’t replace a friend because he’s ill. He accepted the money for the school, on condition that it went through the town hall and that a music room was rebuilt next to the classrooms. The town hall agreed.

In Lyon, Rose-Hélène watched the video ten times. She asked why the ladies were singing. Julien explained that in Corsica people sang for important things: births, weddings, deaths. And sometimes for trees. Rose-Hélène thought about it. Then she asked whether she could send something to the Corsican lime tree. Not water, since it was too far. Something else.

That same evening, under the La Duchère lime tree, during the eight o’clock water distribution, she asked everyone to be quiet. She took out her harmonica. She played the three notes. Then she asked Théo to record them on his phone. Then she asked Inès to play the rest on the clarinet. Then Nadia, on the flute. Then everyone who had brought an instrument. There were a lot of them.

The recording lasted four minutes. It was Henri’s waltz, played by about forty people standing around a tree, with empty buckets at their feet, in the orange evening light. At the third verse they all stopped. Eight bars of silence. And in that silence you could hear only the sound of the water soaking into the dry earth, like a very long sigh.

Théo sent the recording to the music teacher in Corte. The teacher played it to Antoine the next morning on the square, with a small speaker placed on the edge of the fountain. Antoine listened to the end, leaning on his cane. During the silence he closed his eyes. Then he asked the teacher to play it again. And again. He listened to it five times in a row, without a word.

Then he took his bucket and went to the fountain. And that morning, for the first time, he too sang as he watered. Not a Corsican song. He whistled. The first three notes of Henri’s waltz. Off-key, with an old man’s breath. The three women looked at each other. Then the youngest, who was seventy, whistled the next three. And on the blackened square, between the fountain and the dead tree, the waltz went on.

At the beginning of August, Minister Desforges appeared on television. He was asked what the state intended to do about heatwaves. He talked about budgets, plans, figures. Then, at the end, he talked about a Lyon neighbourhood watering its tree with air-conditioner water, and an old Corsican shepherd watering a burnt tree. He announced a national programme: “a tree for every school”. His daughter Clémence, it later emerged, had shown him both videos.

The rain finally came on 16 August. An enormous storm broke over Lyon in the late afternoon, with lightning everywhere and rain so violent that the streets turned into rivers. The La Duchère children ran out into the downpour, laughing, shouting, dancing around the lime tree. Rose-Hélène raised her head to the sky, mouth open, to drink the rain. Like a tree.

That night, for the first time in two months, Henri-Ion slept in his own bed, on the other side of the landing. It was twenty-two degrees. The window was open, and you could hear the rain falling in the courtyard. Rose-Hélène, however, refused to leave Odile’s room. She told Isabelle she had got used to it there, and that anyway, the door stayed open. Isabelle didn’t object.

At Lyon-Part-Dieu station, that same evening, Mr Vidal missed his 21:34 train, then the 22:34. It wasn’t because of the storm, even though all the papers wrote about late trains the next day. It was because he and Amina had stayed under the station canopy, watching the rain, without a word, for an hour and a half. He took the last train, at midnight. He never could explain why.

The next day, Amina closed the water spreadsheet. It contained fifty-four evenings, one thousand three hundred and twelve participants and eleven thousand six hundred and forty litres of air-conditioner water. The La Duchère lime tree had regained almost all its leaves. Dr Lefèvre declared it saved. Thanks to the rain, of course. But above all, she pointed out, thanks to a whole neighbourhood that had refused to let it die.

In Corsica the storm came two days later. Antoine spent the whole storm sitting under the wash house on the square, watching the rain fall on his black tree. He refused to go indoors. The three women brought him a blanket and a coffee. The music teacher later recounted that at one point during the storm Antoine had raised his glass of coffee to the tree, as if clinking glasses with an old friend.

On 22 August, when the roads in Corsica reopened, Julien and Rose-Hélène took the boat to Bastia. Ioana had gone with Sorina to see the burnt school and take measurements. Julien had promised his daughter she could see the tree with her own eyes. Rose-Hélène spent the crossing holding on to the rail, looking at the sea. She asked whether it was the same sea as the one at Marseille, Odile’s sea. Julien said yes.

The village was unrecognisable. The hills around were black as far as the eye could see, with charred tree trunks here and there pointing at the sky like burnt matches. It still smelled of smoke. But on the little square the fountain was running, and someone had put red geraniums in pots on the edge of the wash house. Antoine was sitting on a stone bench next to his black tree, his empty bucket at his feet.

He recognised Rose-Hélène at once, though he had never seen her. He smiled his toothless old shepherd’s smile and beckoned her over. Rose-Hélène walked slowly towards the tree. She looked at the black trunk, the bare branches, the burnt earth. Then she put her hand on the bark, on the side that hadn’t burnt. She stayed like that for a long time, her palm flat, her eyes closed, as if listening.

Then she turned to Antoine. She said, very seriously, that it was alive. That she had felt it. That it was warm on that side, like a hand. Antoine said nothing. He just nodded, slowly, several times. Then he handed her the bucket. Rose-Hélène went to fill it at the fountain, with both hands, spilling half of it. And that day, it was she who watered the Corsican tree.

In the evening, Julien and Rose-Hélène had dinner at the house of the youngest of the three singers, whose home hadn’t burnt. Antoine was there, and the music teacher, and about ten neighbours. They ate brocciu, figs and bread baked over a wood fire. At the end of the meal, the three women sang. Then Antoine asked Rose-Hélène to play the three notes. She played. And the whole table, in Corsican and in French, whistled the rest.

Nobody yet knew whether the Corsican lime tree was alive. They would have to wait until spring. Antoine was ninety-six, and he knew as well as anyone that he wasn’t sure to be there in spring. On the last evening of August, he asked the teacher to write a letter for him, because his hands shook too much. A letter for Rose-Hélène, in Lyon. It was four lines long.

“Dear little one, thank you for the music. My tree heard it. I water it every morning, because of you and thanks to you. If I’m no longer here in spring, come and see if it has leaves. And if it does, whistle the three notes to it. It will know it’s you. Antoine.” Rose-Hélène had her father read the letter to her three times. Then she put it in the box of Henri’s harmonica. She said she would go. In the spring.

Reading: Why is it so hot in cities?

A popular-science article Dr Lefèvre wrote for the town hall magazine. Notice how she explains each cause with a different expression. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Pourquoi fait-il si chaud en ville ?
This summer it was up to six degrees hotter in central Lyon than in the surrounding countryside. This phenomenon has a name: the urban heat island. It has several causes.
First, as concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day, they release it at night. So the city never really cools down, even after sunset.
Next, for lack of sufficient green spaces, water doesn’t evaporate. Yet it is evaporation that cools the air. A single large tree produces as much coolness as five air conditioners.

Finally, the air conditioners themselves make the problem worse, since they discharge into the street the hot air they remove from flats. The hotter it gets, the more people use air conditioning, and the hotter it gets outside.

It’s not that cities are doomed to suffocate. Thanks to trees, green roofs and fountains, the temperature can be brought down by several degrees. By planting and planting, Paris has already gained two degrees in some neighbourhoods.
Given that heatwaves will become more and more frequent because of global warming, every tree planted today is an investment for tomorrow. — Dr Claire Lefèvre, botanist

The causes of an environmental problem

Write (at least 250 words) in French an article explaining the causes of an environmental problem in your town or country (air pollution, floods, disappearing forests, water shortage). At the end, propose a solution. Use at least 7 different expressions of cause.

I used “en raison de” or “du fait de” (formal register).
I used “étant donné que” or “vu que”.
I used “ce n’est pas que” + subjunctive.
Every spring, the town of my childhood floods. As the river overflows more and more often, the residents live in fear.
These floods are explained first by deforestation: for lack of trees on the hills, the rain is no longer held by the earth.
Next, because of concrete, water can no longer soak into the ground. Owing to more violent rainfall linked to global warming, the situation gets worse every year.
It’s not that the authorities are indifferent, but they lack the means.
Given that the problem comes from the hills, so does the solution: by replanting again and again, we could, thanks to the trees’ roots, hold the water where it falls.
